title: Carry an arrow around a loop
makes_visible: An arrow moved without ever being turned comes back turned on a curved surface, but not on a flat or merely bent one. The turn grows with the area the loop encloses and reverses when the loop is walked the other way. It is the one picture behind parallel transport, path dependence, holonomy, Gaussian curvature, and the meaning of the Riemann tensor.

picture.caption: Carry an arrow around a closed path without turning it: on a ball it comes back turned, and on a flat sheet it does not.
picture.composition: A shaded surface with a faint grid fills the scene. A closed path is drawn on it, the region it encloses is lightly tinted, and a small arrowhead on the path shows the walking direction. Faded copies of the carried arrow mark its progress. An inset at the base point shows the starting arrow and the returned arrow side by side, with an arc between them. Readouts for the turn and the enclosed area appear only when the loop closes.

tour.show: Ball with the octant loop from the North Pole down to the equator, a quarter of the way along it, and back. The arrow sits at the pole, pointing down the first path.
tour.say: Here is a ball and a closed path. I will carry this arrow along the path, and I will never turn it.

tour.show: The arrow reaches the equator. The path turns left, and the arrow keeps pointing south.
tour.say: At the corner I turn to follow the path. The arrow does not turn. It keeps pointing the way it was pointing.

tour.show: Back at the pole. The inset shows the starting arrow and the returned arrow, a right angle apart.
tour.say: We are home. Compare the two arrows. The arrow has made a quarter turn, and nobody turned it.

tour.show: Switch to the flat plane and walk a square.
tour.say: Now a walk on a flat floor, with four corners. The arrow comes back exactly as it left.

tour.show: Switch to the tube, walk a loop around it, then open the unrolled view.
tour.say: A rolled-up tube looks curved, but the arrow comes back unturned. Unroll it and you see why. It is a flat sheet.

tour.show: Back on the ball, shrink the loop to half the area. The readout shows half the turn.
tour.say: Fence in half as much of the ball, and the turn is half as big. The turn measures how much curving is inside the loop.

design_rules.rule: Never show a running angle while the arrow is moving.
design_rules.because: Arrows at different places on a curved surface cannot be compared independently of the route; the turn exists only when the loop closes.

design_rules.rule: Keep the plane and the tube one click away from the ball.
design_rules.because: Learners otherwise blame the corners, the walking rule, or mere bending for the turn.

design_rules.rule: Make reversal visibly symmetric: the same path, a mirrored direction arrowhead, and the opposite turn.
design_rules.because: Many learners believe the direction of travel does not matter.

design_rules.rule: On the cone, make loops that miss the tip the easiest thing to draw.
design_rules.because: Seeing them return unchanged, next to a loop around the tip that does not, is the whole lesson about flat regions and non-shrinkable loops.

design_rules.rule: Distinguish start and returned arrows by line style as well as colour.
design_rules.because: Colour alone fails for colour-blind learners and in print.

model.summary: The arrow is carried by integrating the parallel transport equation in the surface's own coordinates. The 3D arrow is drawn by mapping its components through the surface embedding, so the embedding never affects the physics.
equations: \text{cone with deficit angle } \delta:\quad \Delta\alpha = \delta \text{ for loops around the tip, } 0 \text{ otherwise}
model.method: Fourth-order Runge–Kutta in surface coordinates, switching to a rotated chart near coordinate poles. Great-circle legs are cross-checked against exact rotations. Gaussian curvature comes from the metric, and the enclosed curvature is integrated numerically for the readout. Tube and cone use their unrolled flat charts, where transport is translation and the seam identification adds any rotation.

accessibility: Each tour beat has a spoken description of where the arrow points relative to the path: ahead, left, right, or behind. The returned turn is announced in degrees. Every control works from the keyboard, and the static card is the fallback when 3D is unavailable.

starting_material.notes: The earlier course's transport model and its checks can be ported almost unchanged as a TypeScript module, and the two-routes lab becomes a preset of this one. The octant SVG becomes the static card. New work: saddle and cone surfaces, the unrolled views, and the area readouts.
